newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Zanzibar parliament endorses annual budget.
newsitem.headline: Zanzibar parliament endorses annual budget.

text.p: Zanzibar's parliament, boycotted by the opposition over a political dispute, approved government budget proposals for 1997/98, a senior finance ministry official said on Thursday.
The proposals were endorsed on Wednesday with a ministerial pledge to implement more rigorous revenue collection, said Adam Mkwakale, personal assistant to Zanzibar Finance Minister Amina Salum Ali.
The government on the Indian Ocean islands is expected to raise a total of 41.5 billion Tshs ($66.5 million) in revenue, Mkwakale told Reuters.
"Total expenditure for 1997/98 will be 55.5 billion shillings of which 44.6 billion is for recurrent expenditure," he said. A further 12.83 billion Tshs was earmarked for development.

"The discrepancy (between revenue and expenditure) is made up by external assistance from friendly countries and the UNDP (United Nations Development Programme) which is non-political," said a senior diplomat.
Earlier Ali promised tough action against persons convicted of misusing government funds, but gave no furthur details.
Zanzibar's opposition Civic United Front party boycotts
the parliament, claiming 1995 general elections were rigged by the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (Party of the Revolution - CCM).
Special attention would be paid to the island's tourism and petroleum sectors, a major source of revenue collection, Mkwakale said.
The International Monetary Fund's senior representative in Tanzania, Festus Osunsade, gave a cautious endorsement to the budget statement.

"We welcome the interest expressed by the honourable minister to strengthen fiscal discipline on the island," Osunsade told Reuters, adding the IMF also welcomed Zanzibar's intention to introduce a Value Added Tax (VAT) in collaboration with the mainland.
Zanzibar's twin islands joined with Tanganyika to form the Tanzanian Union in 1964, but remains semi-autonomous with a separate parliament and tax base.

According to the latest figures given by the Tanzanian Revenue Authority (TRA), revenue collected from Zanzibar during 1996/97 comprised 93 percent from customs and excise and seven percent from income tax.
Diplomats familiar with Zanzibar's economy warned more effort must be directed at cuts to an overbloated civil service sector.

While comprising only three percent of Tanzania's estimated 30 million population, Zanzibar's civil service wage bill is 5.5 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP), almost double that of the mainland.
"A key element here is civil service reform --what we should be looking for is how much they (Zanzibar) are doing," a senior diplomat said.
"This budget doesn't bring out clearly how they're going to address these problems. Our feeling is they have to begin to manage their budget the way the Union is doing," the diplomat said.
The diplomat added it was unrealistic to expect Zanzibar to embark on mass retrenchments of state workers without support from Western donors.
"No developing country can do a major civil service reform without donor assistance." Donor countries froze most aid to Zanzibar following the 1995 elections.
Mainland Tanzania's budget will be announced in parliament by Finance Minister Daniel Yona on June 19.
